title: Human Expert Evaluation of Agentic AI for EO, form F07
description:
Thank you for helping us evaluate the performance of different LLMs in Agentic AI frameworks for EO!

WHAT THIS IS
We built a benchmark to test the performance of different LLMs in agentic settings. This evaluation form is to compare the answers given by these LLMs when answering a question using different tools related to the agentic framework that we built - including different EO endpoints (Copernicus/Sentinel, Landsat), ERA5 climate data, EO Dashboard narratives, ESA science strategy documents, GIS analysis and scientific literature search.

You will be given 8 questions, and for each question you see every anonymous answer that assistant actually produced for it -- usually several, occasionally just one if only one assistant answered that particular question.

WHAT YOU DO
(About 40 minutes for this form -- your progress is saved in this browser, so it's fine to do this over more than one sitting.) The form will guide you through it, but for every question you will
1. Rate how relevant and realistic the question is for EO users.
2. Score the accuracy of each answer shown.
3. If there's more than one answer, rank them all from best to worst (skip this step when only one answer is shown -- there's nothing to compare it to).

HOW TO JUDGE ACCURACY
Judge scientific and domain correctness, and whether the answer addresses every part of the question. A minority of answers (marked "▣ image" next to the answer letter) include the actual image the assistant looked at -- check the description against it directly. For every other answer you cannot open the files or images it says it produced: treat claims that you find implausible or unsupported as errors. Do not reward length or formatting. If you cannot judge a question, say so in the comment field and give your best estimate.

Answers were produced automatically and may contain errors. Local file paths were removed from the answers. Long answers are collapsed by default — click an answer to expand it.

PRIVACY
Your name is recorded so we can follow up if needed, and is not shown to other experts. Responses are used only for the research evaluation of this benchmark and are reported in aggregate. Participation is voluntary; you can stop at any time by closing the page.

profile_fields.title: Name
profile_fields.help: So we know who a response came from. Not shown to other experts.

profile_fields.title: How would you rate your Earth Observation expertise?
Which areas are you experienced in?
choices: Climate and atmospheric data (ERA5, trace gases)

profile_fields.title: Consent
choices: I agree that my responses are used for the research evaluation of this benchmark.

relevance.title: How relevant and realistic is this question for EO users (researchers, analysts, practitioners)?
relevance.help: 1 = not relevant or unrealistic; 3 = plausible but marginal or somewhat artificial; 5 = highly relevant and realistic.

accuracy.title: Accuracy: how correct and complete is each answer?
accuracy.help: 1 = incorrect or unusable; 2 = mostly incorrect or major omissions; 3 = partially correct or incomplete; 4 = mostly correct, minor issues; 5 = correct and complete. Equal scores are allowed.

ranking.title: Ranking: order all answers from best to worst.
ranking.help: Drag, or use the arrows, to put the best answer at the top and the worst at the bottom. Ties are not allowed.

familiarity.title: How familiar are you with the topic of this question?

comment.title: Comment (optional)
comment.help: For example: an error you spotted, why a question is not relevant, or that you could not judge it.

items.question: Query the EOSS knowledge base for ESA mission objectives related to atmospheric sounding instruments (e.g. infrared sounders and GNSS radio occultation). Based on the target atmospheric layers identified, download hourly ERA5 temperature at the relevant pressure levels, for a representative area and sample period, to contextualise the mission science.

answers.text:
The ESA Earth Observation Science Strategy (EOSS) knowledge base has been queried, and the target atmospheric layers and scientific objectives for infrared sounders and GNSS radio occultation have been identified:

Key Findings from EOSS Knowledge Base
1. Infrared Sounders (e.g., IASI)
• Target Atmospheric Layers:
  • Troposphere (primary focus for water vapor profiling and temperature/humidity retrievals).
  • Stratosphere (secondary focus for limb sounding and trace gas observations).
• Scientific Objectives:
  • Water vapor profiling for climate feedback studies.
  • Climate sensitivity and energy balance analysis.
  • Atmospheric chemistry and composition monitoring.
  • Extreme events and hazards (e.g., aerosol-cloud interactions).

2. GNSS Radio Occultation (GNSS-RO)
• Target Atmospheric Layers:
  • Upper Troposphere to Lower Stratosphere (UTLS) (primary focus for temperature, pressure, and humidity profiling).
  • Ionosphere (secondary focus for electron density and space weather studies).
• Scientific Objectives:
  • High-precision atmospheric profiling for weather forecasting and climate models.
  • Earth energy imbalance studies.
  • Space weather and ionospheric research.
  • Detection of atmospheric pressure waves from extreme events.

items.question: Find an EO Dashboard narrative about climate change impacts, retrieve its full content to identify the study area, select and download an appropriate EO image for that area, and query the ESA Science Strategy for policy context on the same topic. Explain how the selected observation helps assess the climate impact described in the narrative.

answers.text:
The selected Sentinel-2 true-color image of California, USA, provides a visual representation of the region's landscape, which can be used to assess the impact of climate change on wildfires. The image shows a mix of natural and urban areas, with visible patches of vegetation, water bodies, and human settlements. The presence of smoke plumes and burned areas in the image indicates that wildfires have occurred in the region, which is consistent with the narrative from the "WildfireVLM" paper that highlights the increasing frequency and intensity of wildfires due to climate change.

The image helps assess the climate impact described in the narrative by providing a visual confirmation of the wildfire activity in California. The smoke plumes and burned areas in the image are indicative of the effects of climate change on the region, such as increased temperatures and prolonged droughts, which contribute to the occurrence of wildfires. The image also allows for the identification of specific areas that have been affected by wildfires, which can be used to further analyze the impact of climate change on the region.

In summary, the selected observation helps assess the climate impact described in the narrative by providing a visual representation of the wildfire activity in California, which is consistent with the narrative's description of the increasing frequency and intensity of wildfires due to climate change. The image also allows for the identification of specific areas that have been affected by wildfires, which can be used to further analyze the impact of climate change on the region.

The request to retrieve a Sentinel-2 true-color JPEG quicklook for the northwest Pacific Oyashio front region could not be completed due to repeated authentication and tool constraints. However, the EO Dashboard narrative and ESA Earth Observation Science Strategy policy context have been successfully retrieved and analyzed.

Summary of Findings

1. EO Dashboard Narrative: Climate Change Impacts on Ocean Health
• Narrative Title: Understanding climate change effects on water temperature and ocean currents is vital to managing these resources
• Study Area: Northwest Pacific Oyashio front region (approximately 140°E–150°E, 40°N–50°N).
• Key Climate Impact:
  • Phytoplankton bloom timing shifts due to warming: blooms occur later in colder years and earlier in warmer years.
  • This shift disrupts predator-prey dynamics, impacting marine ecosystems and fisheries.
• Satellite Data Used:
  • Ocean color observations (e.g., Sentinel-3 OLCI, VIIRS) to monitor phytoplankton biomass, productivity, and carbon absorption.
  • Sea surface temperature (SST) data to assess thermal changes.

2. ESA Earth Observation Science Strategy: Policy Context
The ESA EO Science Strategy aligns with international frameworks to address climate change impacts on ocean health and marine ecosystems:

• Paris Agreement:
  • Articles 4 & 5: Focus on mitigation, sinks, and reservoirs, including ocean carbon sinks.
  • Article 7: Adaptation strategies for coastal resilience.
  • Science Questions (SQs):
    • SQ-03 (Ocean Carbon Cycle): Addresses ocean sinks and marine ecosystem health.
    • SQ-05 (Coastal Sea Level): Supports adaptation and loss/damage assessments.

• Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD):
  • Articles 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 13: Conservation and sustainable use of biodiversity, including marine ecosystems.
  • SQ-03 (Ocean Carbon Cycle): Supports monitoring of marine ecosystems.

• UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs):
  • SDG 13 (Climate Action): Mitigation and adaptation.
  • SDG 14 (Life Below Water): Conservation of oceans and marine resources.
  • SQ-03 (Ocean Carbon Cycle): Directly supports SDG 14.

• Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction:
  • Priorities 1–4: Understanding risk, governance, resilience, and preparedness for coastal hazards.
  • SQ-05 (Coastal Sea Level): Informs risk reduction.

• EU Green Deal:
  • Net Zero by 2050: Climate neutrality and decarbonization.
  • Ecosystems and Biodiversity: Protection of marine and coastal ecosystems.

3. How Satellite Observations Help Assess Climate Impacts
• Ocean Color (Sentinel-3 OLCI, VIIRS):
  • Tracks phytoplankton blooms, which are sensitive to temperature and nutrient changes.
  • Provides early warnings of ecosystem disruptions (e.g., shifts in bloom timing).
• Sea Surface Temperature (SST):
  • Monitors thermal changes driving bloom shifts and marine heatwaves.
• Policy Relevance:
  • Paris Agreement: Supports MRV (Measurement, Reporting, Verification) for carbon sinks and adaptation.
  • CBD: Enables monitoring of biodiversity and ecosystem health.
  • SDG 14: Provides data for sustainable fisheries and marine conservation.

Next Steps
If you'd like, I can:
1. Attempt to retrieve Sentinel-3 OLCI ocean color data for the Oyashio region to analyze phytoplankton blooms.
2. Perform GIS analysis (e.g., NDVI, zonal statistics) on any downloaded imagery to quantify changes.
3. Use the VLM agent to visually inspect any available images for cloud cover, bloom presence, or other features.

items.label: Cross-agent Synthesis
items.question: Search the EO Dashboard for narratives related to extreme weather events and early-warning applications. Select a relevant event, extract the study area and event period from the narrative, and search the EOSS knowledge base for ESA science strategy objectives related to extreme weather monitoring and prediction. Based on the identified event, retrieve a suitable ERA5 pressure-level variable (e.g., 500 hPa geopotential height or 250 hPa wind) over the corresponding region and period. Visualize the ERA5 field and explain how the observed atmospheric dynamics relate to the extreme event and the ESA science objectives.

answers.text:
Here is the Python code to visualize the ERA5 500 hPa geopotential height data for East Africa during April–May 2024. This code will:
1. Load the NetCDF file.
2. Calculate the mean geopotential height.
3. Create a visualization with a filled contour map, contour lines, geographic boundaries, a colorbar, and a title.
4. Save the visualization as a PNG file.

Python Code

import xarray as xr
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import cartopy.crs as ccrs
import cartopy.feature as cfeature

Load the NetCDF file
file_path = "era5_500hPa_geopotential_april_may_2024_east_africa.nc"
ds = xr.open_dataset(file_path)

Calculate the mean geopotential height for the period
mean_geopotential = ds["z"].mean(dim="valid_time") / 9.81  # Convert to geopotential height (meters)

Create the visualization
plt.figure(figsize=(12, 8))
ax = plt.axes(projection=ccrs.PlateCarree())
ax.set_extent([29, 51, -12, 5], crs=ccrs.PlateCarree())

Filled contour map
contourf = mean_geopotential.plot.contourf(
    ax=ax,
    transform=ccrs.PlateCarree(),
    cmap="viridis",
    levels=20,
    add_colorbar=False
)

Contour lines
contour = mean_geopotential.plot.contour(
    ax=ax,
    transform=ccrs.PlateCarree(),
    colors="white",
    linewidths=0.8,
    levels=20
)
plt.clabel(contour, inline=True, fontsize=8, fmt="%1.0f")

Add geographic boundaries
ax.add_feature(cfeature.COASTLINE, linewidth=0.8)
ax.add_feature(cfeature.BORDERS, linestyle=":", linewidth=0.5)
ax.add_feature(cfeature.LAND, color="lightgray")
ax.add_feature(cfeature.OCEAN, color="lightcyan")

Add colorbar
cbar = plt.colorbar(contourf, ax=ax, orientation="vertical", pad=0.05, shrink=0.7)
cbar.set_label("Geopotential Height (m)", fontsize=10)

Add title
plt.title("ERA5 500 hPa Geopotential Height - East Africa (April–May 2024)", fontsize=12, pad=20)

Save the visualization
output_path = "era5_500hPa_geopotential_april_may_2024_east_africa.png"
plt.savefig(output_path, dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.show()

print(f"Visualization saved to: {output_path}")

Output
The visualization will be saved as:

era5_500hPa_geopotential_april_may_2024_east_africa.png

How to Run the Code
1. Ensure you have the required Python libraries installed:

   pip install xarray matplotlib cartopy netCDF4

2. Copy the code above into a Python script (e.g., visualize_era5.py).
3. Run the script:

   python visualize_era5.py

Interpretation of the Visualization
• Ridges (high geopotential height): Indicate stable, dry conditions and are often associated with blocking high-pressure systems.
• Troughs (low geopotential height): Indicate unstable, wet conditions and are linked to storm development and heavy rainfall.
• Anomalies: Deviations from the climatological mean can highlight unusual atmospheric conditions that contributed to the extreme weather event (e.g., El Niño-induced floods and Cyclone Hidaya).

Relation to ESA EO Science Strategy
The visualization aligns with the ESA Earth Observation Science Strategy (EOSS) objectives, particularly:
1. Science Theme ST-V: Extremes and Hazards – Improving prediction and monitoring of extreme weather events.
2

Strategic Context of the Paris Agreement (PARIS) in the ESA EO Science Strategy:
The Paris Agreement is a cornerstone of the ESA Earth Observation Science Strategy, aligning EO science with global policy frameworks to maximize societal benefits. Its key articles—Article 4 (Mitigation), Article 5 (Sinks and Reservoirs), Article 7 (Adaptation), Article 8 (Loss and Damage), Article 12 (Public Engagement), Article 13 (Transparency), and Article 14 (Global Stocktake)—are directly supported by ESA's science questions (SQs) and strategic objectives.

Key Links:
• Mitigation (Article 4): Supported by SQs like SQ-01 (Global carbon cycle), SQ-45 (Climate sensitivity), and SQ-48 (Planetary heat exchange), which provide data for monitoring GHG sinks, reservoirs, and emission reduction strategies.
• Adaptation (Article 7): Addressed by SQs such as SQ-05 (Coastal sea level) and SQ-21 (Drivers of sea-ice state), aiding coastal risk management and adaptation planning.
• Transparency and Global Stocktake (Articles 13 & 14): EO science underpins the Enhanced Transparency Framework (ETF) through SQ-01 and SQ-02 (Land biosphere responses), enabling accurate carbon accounting and progress tracking toward Net Zero.

The strategy explicitly maps Science Questions (SQs) to the Paris Agreement, demonstrating how EO science informs its implementation. For example:
• SQ-01 (Global carbon cycle) and SQ-02 (Land biosphere responses) have a strength of link = 3 to the Paris Agreement, directly supporting mitigation, adaptation, and transparency.
